cur:catacombs-split-good-shepherd-sarcop.summary: Columns and a central gabled aedicula articulate the front: in the middle the Good Shepherd stands with a sheep on his shoulders, flanked by the deceased couple in the side niches and by crowds of small figures. The tomb comes from Salona, the great early Christian centre of Dalmatia.
facts: It comes from Salona and is dated by Commons to about 300–330.
Salona, near Split, was the capital of Roman Dalmatia and the seat of an important early Christian community.
cur:catacombs-split-good-shepherd-sarcop.notes: The Good Shepherd is a symbolic image of Christ; here the Christian context of the Salona cemeteries supports the identification.

cur:monumental-naples-baptistery-samarit.summary: Two water miracles are set side by side: at the left Christ sits beside a striped well-head, his head lost but his outstretched arm reaching over the well towards the Samaritan woman, who stands frontally holding up a small bucket; behind her stand the six water jars of Cana, into which two servants pour from amphorae. Both stories spoke directly to the newly baptised about the 'living water' and the transforming power of Christ.
facts: Of the scenes once set within garlands around the dome, four survive: the Traditio Legis, the Samaritan woman with the Wedding at Cana, the Miraculous Draught (or Peter on the water), and the women at the tomb.

The baptistery of San Giovanni in Fonte beside Naples Cathedral is one of the oldest in the West; its building is dated to the 4th century, and its construction is attributed to Bishop Severus (362–408) or to later bishops.

cur:monumental-naples-baptistery-samarit.notes: Christ's head and shoulders are lost; only his seated body and arm survive at the left. The Commons file names this 'nozze di Cana' (Wedding at Cana).

cur:monumental-oberzell-stilling-storm.summary: A great golden boat crowded with apostles tosses on a pale blue sea; within it Christ appears twice, once asleep and once rising to rebuke the wind and waves, while a sail billows above. A Latin verse inscription runs along the lower border, as beneath each scene of the cycle.
facts: The eight miracle scenes on the nave walls of St George, Oberzell, were rediscovered under later plaster in 1880; they are dated either to about 900 (late Carolingian) or, in the prevailing view, to the late 10th century (Ottonian).

Apart from Müstair, St George is the only church north of the Alps in the former Empire to preserve so complete a cycle of early medieval wall painting; the sequence runs from the entrance along the north wall to the altar and back along the south wall, culminating in the Raising of Lazarus.
In each scene Christ, larger than the other figures, stands at the left with a gesture of blessing directed into the narrative, except in two scenes where he appears twice.

met:468764.summary: This tiny engraved gem, less than 2 cm high, is catalogued by the Metropolitan Museum as showing Christ before the elders; worn shapes of a larger draped figure and a smaller one can be made out in the translucent chalcedony. Intaglios like this were cut to be set in rings and used as seals, so that an owner could carry and impress a sacred image in daily life.
facts: The gem measures only about 1.9 × 1.6 cm and came to the Met in 1881 as a gift of John Taylor Johnston, the museum's first president.
Engraved gems (intaglios) were carved in reverse so that, pressed into wax or clay, they left a positive image; Christian subjects on gems appear from the 3rd–4th century onward.
met:468764.notes: The subject cannot be confirmed from the photographs: the engraving is worn and small, and the Met offers no published description. Identification rests on the Met's title alone. The scripture passage is uncertain ('elders' might mean the Sanhedrin, or the boy Jesus among the teachers, Luke 2:41–52), so none is given.
